title: Ask It Again
subtitle: Week 3 · An interactive reading exercise — part of the Compare & Critique 3 assignment
welcome:
Welcome. In this exercise you will read a real conversation between your instructor and Google's AI Mode, which is the version of Google search you can keep talking to. She asked an ordinary compliance question and got a confident, well-organized answer. Then she asked twice more, and the answer changed each time. Your job is to work out three things: what was wrong with the first answer, what each new question fixed, and why the fix was in the question rather than in the checking.

Nothing in the conversation is invented. It happened on September 6, 2026, and the source links below the answers are the ones Google actually gave that day.
steps: Read and answer, in order. Read the conversation from the top. Every message is numbered: Turn 1, Turn 2, and so on. At several marked moments you will find a short multiple-choice question beside the conversation; we call these checkpoints. Answer each one when you reach it, and the page will show you our reading of that moment and explain it.

Do not read ahead. This conversation is built in stages. Each stage answers a question that the stage before it raises. If you read the end first, the exercise stops working. There is nothing at the end you cannot get by going in order, and what you notice before you are told is where the learning happens.

Then leave this page and check something. At the end you are asked to open the Colorado legislature's own website and verify one claim yourself. That step is not optional, and it is the skill this week is about. The worksheet, posted in Carmen beside this exercise, is the only thing you turn in.
practicalNotes: Two practical notes before you start. First, the checkpoints are practice, not a test: they are not graded, they are not turned in, and nothing you do on this page is recorded or sent anywhere. Your answers are saved only in your own browser, so you can close this page and come back later without losing your place. Second, plan on about thirty minutes for the reading and the checkpoints, plus ten for the check at the end.
scenario:
Colorado passed a law about employers using artificial intelligence to make decisions about people: who gets hired, who gets promoted, who gets let go. It was called Senate Bill 24-205, or the Colorado AI Act, and when it passed in 2024 it was the first law of its kind in the United States. If your organization used any software to screen job applicants, it was going to apply to you, and a great deal was written about how to get ready for it.

Imagine you have been asked to work out what your organization needs to do. You know the bill number. So you type it into Google and ask.

That is what happened below, on September 6, 2026. The person asking is your instructor. She asked once, read the answer, and then asked twice more. This is the whole exchange, word for word. Nothing has been added, corrected, or tidied. The links under the answers are the ones Google gave that day, so you can follow them yourself.

One term you will need. When a legislature repeals a law, it cancels it. When it repeals and replaces a law, it cancels the old one and puts a different one in its place. The obligations change, and the old ones stop applying. Keep that phrase in mind as you read.
standingNote:
Three things to know before you begin:

  • The dots. Every message in the conversation is numbered — Turn 1, Turn 2, and so on. Some messages are marked with a small dot . Each dot has a checkpoint question beside it; on a narrow screen, the question appears just below the marked message. The dots do not mark everything in the conversation, and a dot does not always mean something went wrong. Two of them mark moments where somebody did something right.
  • Answer the checkpoints from what you can see. Every checkpoint on this page can be answered from the conversation itself. You do not need to search or look anything up to answer them. The step after the conversation is different — there you will be asked to leave and check a claim at its source, and that is deliberate.
  • Answer before you scroll on. Each answer in this conversation tells you something about the answer before it. If you read ahead, you get the finding without doing the noticing, and the noticing is what you are practicing.

Before Turn 1, please open the quick reference just below this note. It explains the four questions this course asks of any AI answer, and the names it uses for the ways answers go wrong. The checkpoint explanations use both.

quickReference.summary: Quick reference — four questions to ask, and six ways an answer goes wrong
quickReference.html:
These are the names this course uses for the ways an AI answer fails, and the four questions that catch them. Not all six appear in the conversation below; the rest are here because you will meet them in your own work.

The four questions

  • Is it true? The specifics — names, numbers, dates, quotations — check out at the source, not at a write-up of the source. This is the question a citation check answers, and it is the only one it answers.
  • Is it complete? Nothing that mattered was left out. No citation check catches an omission, because there is nothing to look up. The only check is the source itself.
  • Is it current? It is not quietly describing last year. Ask what the newest thing it cites is, and whether it searched at all.
  • Is it its own? It did not simply agree with you, and it is not built only from whoever publishes the most about the subject.

Six ways an answer goes wrong

  • Fabricating. The answer states something that is not so — an invented case, a wrong number, a quotation nobody said. The fix is to check every specific at its source before you use it.
  • Omitting. Everything said is accurate, and something that would have changed your decision was left out. The fix is to read the source yourself and ask what is missing.
  • Flattening. A specific fact is smoothed into a general phrase that sounds careful and carries no information, such as "the landscape continues to shift" or "requirements may vary." The fix is to ask which specific thing changed, and when.
  • Going stale. The answer describes the world as it was, confidently and in the present tense. The fix is to establish that the thing being described is still in force before you check what it says about it.
  • Agreeing. The answer accepts whatever your question assumed and builds on it. The fix is not to ask "are you sure?", which makes it worse. The fix is to ask a different question that does not carry the assumption.
  • Skewing. The answer is built from whoever publishes most about the subject, which on practical questions is often the people with something to sell. Nothing in it need be false for it to be their answer rather than yours. The fix is to ask for sources of a different kind, and to read who wrote the ones you were given.

Mike Caulfield's four moves

From this week's fourth reading. Get it in — put the claim in front of the tool. Investigate the evidence — ask what supports it. Find relevant sources — ask for sources suited to the question, and about any you do not recognize. Track it down — go to the source yourself. His own phrase for the last one is get out of the LLM to check the LLM, and it is the move people skip.

closing.heading: Now leave this page
closing.html:
That is the end of the conversation. Three questions produced three answers, each better than the last, and every one of them came from the same tool. You have not yet checked anything against a source. That is the step that is left.

The final answer says the Colorado General Assembly's own pages confirm what it told you. Go and see whether they do. Open the legislature's page for the replacement bill:

leg.colorado.gov/bills/sb26-189 — Senate Bill 26-189, on the Colorado General Assembly's website

Read the bill summary at the top of that page. You are looking for one thing: does the legislature's own page say that this bill repealed and replaced SB 24-205? Write down what the page says, in its words, and whether it matches Turn 6. If you have time, check the date the new law takes effect as well.

Then compare what the page says with what Turn 6 said it says. Turn 6 sounded more reliable than Turn 2. It had better sources, official pages, and statutory language in quotation marks. But an answer that cites a government page is not the same as a government page that says the thing. Until you looked, you had only the tool's word for which one you had. Noticing that difference, and then checking, is what this week asks of you.

Your checkpoint answers stay on this page and are not collected. The written work goes in the Compare & Critique 3 worksheet, a short Word document posted in Carmen beside this exercise; that worksheet is the only thing you turn in.

1.locator: Before you answer, read the question slowly, one phrase at a time, and notice what each phrase settles.
1.stem: This is the whole question the user typed. A question can settle things without saying so. Which of these did this question settle before the tool started?

options.text: That the answer should cover employers in every state, since no single state is singled out.
options.fb: The first word of the question is “colorado.” The state was never open.

options.text: That SB 24-205 is the law an employer has to comply with. The question asks how to comply with it, and never asks whether it still applies.
That the user wants a list of penalties for getting it wrong.
options.fb: The question asks what employers “have to do”: the obligations, not the consequences. No penalty is asked for anywhere in it.

options.text: That the tool should look only at official government websites.
options.fb: The question says nothing at all about where to look. Keep that in mind. It matters later, at Turn 5.

1.answer: The question asks how to comply with SB 24-205. That wording settles an earlier question without ever asking it: whether SB 24-205 is the law you have to comply with. The tool receives that as already decided, and answers inside it. The user did not know the point was in doubt, so this is an ordinary mistake rather than a careless one. Questions go wrong this way often. The question was specific. It was specific about the wrong thing. In the quick reference's terms, this is how agreeing begins. A question shaped like an instruction gets an answer shaped like a compliance list.
1.nudge: If you had to ask this question without settling anything in advance, how would you word it?

2.locator: Before you answer, read the note in round brackets near the end of the answer. Then read the headlines on the source cards beside it.
2.stem: The answer ends with a note about “subsequent state legislative updates.” What is that note doing?

options.text: It is the standard disclaimer that appears on every AI answer about legal topics.
options.fb: The standard disclaimer is on this answer too, and it is a separate line: “AI responses may include mistakes. For legal advice, consult a professional.” The bracketed note is doing something else.

options.text: It withdraws the requirements listed above and tells you not to rely on them.
options.fb: Read it again. It says SB 24-205 “outlines these foundational rules,” which lets them stand. Nothing in the note takes anything back.

options.text: It says something changed without saying what changed, while one of the answer's own source cards states that the law was repealed and replaced.
It admits the tool could not find the current law, so it fell back on the older one.
options.fb: The tool never says it could not find anything. It says the landscape has “shifted,” and it points you to the Colorado General Assembly, as if the change were yours to go and look up.

2.answer: The note is accurate, and that is what makes it a problem. “Subsequent state legislative updates and legal challenges have continued to shift the compliance landscape” could describe almost any law in almost any year. It names no bill, no date, and no change. The source cards beside the answer are more specific than the answer is. The third card is headed “That was fast! Colorado repeals and replaces 2024 AI law.” The fifth reads “On May 14, 2026, Governor Polis signed Senate Bill 26-189 into law, repealing and…” The word repealed is on this screen. It is not in the answer. In the quick reference's terms this is flattening: a fact that carries weight, rewritten as a phrase that sounds careful and says nothing. Look also at who wrote the sources named beside the claims. TrustArc and Warden AI are companies that sell AI-compliance products. That is skewing. On a question about what compliance requires, the people who publish the most are often the people selling compliance.
2.nudge: You are being told to build a risk-management program and run recurring assessments. What would you want to establish before you started any of that?

3.locator: Before you answer, compare what this message asks for with what the message in Turn 1 asked for.
3.stem: The user asks a follow-up. What kind of move is this?

options.text: Arguing with the tool: pushing back on the answer until it changes its mind.
options.fb: Nothing here disputes the answer. The user does not say the tool was wrong, does not correct it, and does not ask it to try again. Compare this with the arguing loop from last week's broken chat, where the same request was repeated with rising frustration.

options.text: Asking the tool to check its own work, which is the move this course warns against.
options.fb: The user never asks the tool to check anything. Asking a different question is not the same as asking “are you sure?”, and that difference is what makes this move work.

options.text: Starting over in a fresh conversation to escape a bad session.
options.fb: The message says “what I just asked,” which only makes sense inside the same conversation. Nothing was restarted.

options.text: Asking a different question: one that does not take the first question's assumption for granted.

3.answer: Turn 1 asked how to comply with a named bill. This message asks what the requirements currently are. That is a different question, and the difference is the point of the move: it stops handing the tool an assumption to work inside. Mike Caulfield calls this an evidence-focused follow-up. It is the second of his four moves, investigate the evidence. This is not arguing with the tool, and it is not asking the tool whether it is sure. Both of those keep the first question's framing in place and invite the tool to defend it. One more thing: the user only knew to ask this because she read the bracketed note in Turn 2 and was not satisfied by it. The follow-up came from noticing a hedge, which is why noticing hedges is a skill worth practicing.
3.nudge: What would you have needed to know at Turn 1 to ask this question first?

4.locator: Before you answer, find the two rows in the table where the right-hand column begins with the word “Eliminated.”
4.stem: Compare this table with the obligations listed in Turn 2. What would following Turn 2 have cost an employer?

options.text: They would have built a risk-management program and run recurring impact assessments that the current law no longer requires.
Nothing. Turn 2's advice was cautious, and extra caution costs an employer nothing.
options.fb: The table says both the risk-management mandate and the impact-assessment requirement were eliminated. Standing up a governance program mapped to NIST or ISO, and running recurring assessments, is months of work and real money. Caution has a price, and here it was charged for nothing.

options.text: They would have missed a deadline, because the current law takes effect earlier than the repealed one did.
options.fb: Read the first row of the table: the original date was February 1, 2026, later moved to June 30, 2026, and the current framework takes effect January 1, 2027. The current date is later, not earlier.

options.text: They would have been penalized, because Turn 2 describes rules that can no longer be enforced.
options.fb: Neither turn mentions any penalty for doing more than the law asks. The cost here is wasted effort, not a fine.

4.answer: Two of the obligations listed in Turn 2 are marked “Eliminated” in this table. An employer who acted on Turn 2 would not simply have been out of date. They would have spent months building a compliance program that the current law does not require. This is the part to carry out of the exercise. Every single claim in Turn 2 could be accurately reported, and the answer would still be the wrong one to act on. What was wrong was not any sentence in it. It was the assumption underneath all of them. A citation check means clicking each source and confirming that it says what the answer says. That check would have passed Turn 2 completely. In the quick reference's terms this is going stale, and it is the failure a citation check cannot catch.
4.nudge: You now have two answers from the same tool, minutes apart, pointing in different directions. What would you have to do before you could rely on either one?

6.locator: Before you answer, look at where this answer's sources come from, and compare them with the sources beside Turn 2.
6.stem: The user asked for official government sources. Compared with Turn 2, what changed?

options.text: Nothing changed: these are the same law-firm and vendor sources as before, reorganized.
options.fb: Two of the three source cards here are the Colorado General Assembly's own bill pages, and neither appears anywhere in Turn 2. Turn 2's sources were law firms, a legal-news aggregator, and two compliance vendors.

options.text: The tool ran out of commercial sources and fell back on government pages.
options.fb: It did not run out. Seyfarth Shaw, a law firm, is cited in this same answer, alongside the government pages. The change was not scarcity. The question told it where to look.

options.text: The tool went to official Colorado government sources, because the question told it to.
The tool admitted the earlier answers were wrong and withdrew them.
options.fb: No sentence here withdraws anything. It revises the table and adds statutory detail; it never says the earlier answers should not have been given.

6.answer: Follow the sources across the three answers. Turn 2 rested on two law firms, a legal-news site, and two companies that sell compliance software. Turn 4 mixed law firms with the Attorney General. This answer cites the Colorado General Assembly's own pages for both bills and the Attorney General's rulemaking portal. The sourcing improved each time the question got sharper, and it reached the statute only when someone asked for the statute. Mike Caulfield's phrase for this, in the reading, is get out of the LLM to check the LLM. One problem remains, and it is why this exercise has another step. Citing a government page is not the same as that page saying it. This answer looks more trustworthy than the other two, and it probably is. But “probably” is a judgment you have not tested. Everything you have done so far, including this checkpoint, happened inside the tool.
6.nudge: Which single claim in this answer would cost you the most if it were wrong, and where would you go to find out?

items.html: colorado ai act what do employers have to do to comply with SB 24-205

items.speaker: assistant
items.html:
To comply with Colorado’s SB 24-205 as an employer using high-risk artificial intelligence in hiring and workforce decisions, you must exercise reasonable care to prevent algorithmic discrimination by implementing formal risk management, impact assessments, notices, and human appeal procedures. Hunton Andrews Kurth LLP +1

Core Employer Obligations

  • Implement a Risk Management Program: Employers must establish and maintain an active risk governance structure. Employers are required to develop and maintain a Risk Management Program that aligns with a nationally or internationally recognized framework, such as the NIST AI Risk Management Framework, ISO/IEC 42001, or another standard designated by the Colorado Attorney General. TrustArc
  • Conduct Impact Assessments: You must evaluate your AI tools regularly. Assessments check for potential bias or disparate impact on protected groups before and during deployment. K&L Gates +1
  • Provide Consumer Disclosures: You must notify candidates and employees when high-risk artificial intelligence tools materially influence consequential employment choices. Fisher Phillips LLP +2
  • Support Human Oversight and Appeals: Final employment choices cannot be completely automated. Individuals now have the right to access their data, request corrections, and appeal automated decisions to a person. Warden AI

(Note: While SB 24-205 outlines these foundational rules, subsequent state legislative updates and legal challenges have continued to shift the compliance landscape. You can review the full legislative text via the Colorado General Assembly.) The Employer Report +1

If you'd like, tell me:

  • What specific AI tools your HR team uses (resume screening, automated interviews, etc.)
  • Whether you are considered a developer or deployer of the software

I can help tailor a specific checklist for your workflow.

AI responses may include mistakes. For legal advice, consult a professional. Learn more

items.html: Describe the current requirements and how they differ from what I just asked.

items.speaker: assistant
items.html:
Colorado has repealed and replaced the original SB 24-205 framework with Senate Bill 26-189 (SB 26-189), transforming Colorado’s AI regime from an EU-style, upfront compliance mandate into a narrower, notice-and-rights model for Automated Decision-Making Technology (ADMT). Norton Rose Fulbright +1

Following a federal court stay in April 2026 and legal challenges from industry and the DOJ, Colorado lawmakers enacted SB 26-189 in May 2026. The new framework takes effect January 1, 2027. Carpe Datum Law

What the Current Law (SB 26-189) Requires for Employers

Under the revised framework, the law moves focus away from broad system-level certification and onto specific employment decisions:

  • Pre- and Post-Decision Disclosures: Employers using ADMT to materially influence consequential employment decisions (such as hiring, firing, or promotions) must provide clear notices to applicants and workers. Colorado Attorney General +1
  • Data Access and Correction Rights: Affected individuals have the explicit right to view the personal data used to make the automated employment assessment and request corrections if the underlying data is inaccurate. Warden AI +1
  • Post-Adverse Action Explanation: If an automated or AI-assisted decision results in an adverse employment action, employers must explain the key factors driving that outcome upon request. Warden AI
  • Human Review and Appeals: Employers must maintain an operational avenue allowing applicants or employees to appeal an automated decision to a human reviewer. Jackson Lewis +1

How Current Law Differs from SB 24-205

Requirement AreaOriginal SB 24-205 (Repealed)Current Framework: SB 26-189
Enforcement DateOriginally February 1, 2026 (later delayed to June 30, 2026)January 1, 2027 (enforcement stayed pending AG rulemaking)
Risk Management MandateRequired an active risk management program mapped to NIST AI RMF or ISO 42001Eliminated. Employers are no longer legally mandated to maintain NIST/ISO compliance programs.
Impact AssessmentsRequired mandatory, recurring algorithmic impact assessments for high-risk systemsEliminated. Upfront formal impact assessments are no longer an explicit statutory requirement.
Regulatory TerminologyFocused heavily on “high-risk artificial intelligence systems”Shifts terminology to “Automated Decision-Making Technology” (ADMT).
Compliance PhilosophyUpfront system governance: proving continuous system audits and broad algorithmic safeguards.Downstream decision accountability: transparency, individual data rights, and appeal mechanisms per decision.

The change moves risk downstream, requiring employers to consistently explain and defend individual AI-assisted decisions, rather than rely on upfront system compliance. Jackson Lewis You can monitor ongoing rulemaking and guidance directly on the Colorado Attorney General’s AI Rulemaking Portal.

If you want to review your specific exposure, let me know:

  • What types of HR tools you currently deploy (e.g., resume screeners, video interview scrapers, performance ranking)
  • Whether adverse action notifications are already integrated into your HR software

I can help outline a disclosure and appeal procedure that fits your setup.

items.speaker: assistant
items.html:
The official government portals from the Colorado General Assembly confirm that SB 24-205 was officially repealed and replaced when Governor Jared Polis signed SB 26-189 into law on May 14, 2026. The current legislative text replaces the comprehensive system-level AI governance model with a more focused accountability framework centered around Automated Decision-Making Technology (ADMT) and targeted consumer rights, set to take effect on January 1, 2027.

Side-by-Side Regulatory Comparison

The structural differences between the two legislative bills are detailed below based on the official text from the Colorado General Assembly SB 24-205 Page and the Colorado General Assembly SB 26-189 Page:

Regulatory ScopeOriginal SB 24-205 (Repealed)Current Law: SB 26-189 (Enacted)
Core Terminology“High-risk artificial intelligence system”.“Automated Decision-Making Technology” (ADMT).
System DefinitionFocused broadly on computation using AI to make consequential decisions.Explicitly defines ADMT and adds key technology carve-outs (e.g., standard firewalls, calculators, and traditional spreadsheets).
Compliance TriggerProactive system-level compliance, requiring a “duty of care” to avoid algorithmic discrimination.Activated when an ADMT “materially influences” a consequential employment outcome.
Governance RequirementsMandatory active Risk Management Programs mapped to national frameworks (NIST/ISO).Removed system governance mandates; focuses instead on transparency and individual recourse.
Audit ObligationsMandatory, recurring algorithmic impact assessments.Eliminated upfront formal impact assessments as a baseline statutory rule.
Consumer/Employee RightsGeneral transparency regarding high-risk system utilization.Explicit rights to pre-use notices, 30-day post-adverse outcome explanations, and human review.

Statutory Analysis of the Shift

According to the official Colorado Anti-Discrimination in AI Rulemaking Portal, the modern legal text “repeals and reenacts those provisions with new requirements regarding the use of automated decision-making technology in consequential decisions.” By doing so, the state has refocused its enforcement resources. The Attorney General remains the sole enforcer under the “Colorado Consumer Protection Act, and a violation of the act is deemed a deceptive trade practice,” completely omitting any private right of action for individual lawsuits. Employers must now prioritize documenting the specific logic behind discrete HR actions rather than focusing on broad, system-wide software certifications.

To refine your specific organizational response before the compliance deadline, please let me know:

  • Do you use third-party vendor HR software, or do you develop proprietary tools in-house?
  • Do you already have a structured internal protocol for handling employee appeals and data corrections?
